newsitem.title: USA: G7 ministers provide little forex market fodder.
newsitem.headline: G7 ministers provide little forex market fodder.

text.p: Currency traders hoping for some business-boosting market volatility are likely to find little joy in this weekend's discussions by finance ministers and central bankers from major industrial nations.

Finance and monetary officials from the Group of Seven nations touched on a broad range of issues on Saturday and Sunday, including debt relief for poor countries, Europe's plans for a single currency and the need to avoid complacency on the inflation front.
As expected however, they went out of their way to avoid rattling what in recent months has developed into a comfortable state of currency market stability.

"The (currency) market was expecting very neutral G7 statements and it appears that that's what they got," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long Term Credit Bank of Japan. "When all is said and done, there's not much there for the markets to sink their teeth into."

G7 officials "welcomed developments in exchange markets over the recent period" and reaffirmed a commitment to "cooperate closely" on the exchange rate front, according to a statement released by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin after Saturday meetings came to a close.

Finance ministers from other G7 nations echoed Rubin's statement and stressed the need for a strong dollar. They fell short of arguing for a further strengthening in the greenback from current levels.

Analysts noted that France failed France to call for a stronger dollar, as some in the market had expected. This could do some modest damage to the U.S. currency's recent gains versus Europe, they said..
The dollar posted ample gains last week despite the Federal Reserve's decision to keep short-term U.S. interest rates unchanged. It closed at around 1.5240 marks on Friday.

"The fact that (French Finance Minister Jean) Arthuis has not called for a stronger dollar does not give us much fuel for an extension of the dollar rally," said Lisa Finstrom, currency analyst at Smith Barney.

However, Finstrom said any weakness versus European currencies would likely be fleeting and predicted some dollar strength versus the yen on the heels of ostensibly conciliatory talks between the U.S. and Japan.
After the G7 meeting on Saturday, Rubin said the Japanese seemed committed to policies to keep growth going in their country.
"I certainly came away satisfied," Rubin said. "They are very focused on the importance of having an appropriate mix of fiscal and monetary policies to maintain growth."
Analysts had expected harsher rhetoric from the U.S. in pushing Japan to stimulate its economy. A stronger Japanese economy would boost U.S. exports to Japan, easing the bilateral trade deficit.

"I'm a little bit skeptical about degree of comfort on that front but it's important that leaders gave a verbal sign they are talking," said Finstrom. "The fact that there was a vision of cooperation ... could be dollar supportive."

Economists said Rubin's comments suggested that Japan is a long way away from raising interest rates, which would be dollar/yen supportive. On the whole however, they were expecting only modest exchange rate movements to result from the talks.
"What we've seen from the G7 reflects the fact that they don't want to do anything to rattle currency markets," said Robert Hormats, vice chairman at Goldman Sachs (International).

"The U.S. doesn't want the dollar to go up a lot, because then they'll get more angry letters from Detroit (auto manufacturers) and they don't want it to get down because it would adversely affect the U.S. bond market."
Hormats also downplayed suggestions that discussion of Europe's single currency plans will take on a more prominent role at future G7 meetings.
"At this point the debate is really a very European debate," he said. "I think it doesn't help for the G7 to take it up becasue they're not going to add much."
